html:
Muscat and Oman was the sultanate in south-eastern Arabia, under close British protection, from 1856 to 1970. It is the forerunner of today's Sultanate of Oman. The map shows it from 1920 to 1938.

It was born from a split. The Omani Empire of Said bin Sultan stretched from Arabia to East Africa. When he died in 1856 his sons divided it: one took the Sultanate of Zanzibar in Africa, another took Muscat and Oman. Without Zanzibar's trade the Arabian half grew poor. The Al Said sultans held the coast, while the tribes of the interior followed their own Ibadi imam. A rising in 1913 led to the Treaty of Seeb of 1920, which left the interior to the Imamate of Oman in all but name.

The sultanate also held Gwadar on the coast of what is now Pakistan, until it sold it to Pakistan in 1958. Sultan Said bin Taimur (1932 to 1970) kept the country closed and poor even after oil exports began in 1967. In 1970 his son Qaboos overthrew him with British help, renamed the state Oman and began rapid modernisation.
